power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: As the present work reports a secondary data analysis, simulation-based sensitivity power analyses were conducted to identify the minimum detectable effect size (MDES) with approximately 80% power (Table 1). Because the zero-variance exclusions described above yielded emotion-specific analytic samples, power analyses were conducted separately for each emotion that survived the descriptive and floor check, using that emotion's own fitted model structure. This preserved that emotion's specific sample size, residual variance, and random-slope variance. I estimated statistical power across a range of hypothetical true effect sizes (i.e., b = 0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30) for both the pooled synchrony estimate (Model A) and the condition interaction term (Model B) using 1,000 simulations per emotion, per model, and per tested effect size. A second, fine-tuned power analysis was conducted for Model A for the range in which the power estimate crossed .80. This second round of power analyses used the same model structure, but estimated across a narrower range of hypothetical true effect sizes (i.e., b = 0.06 -0.11, Δ = 0.005). A similar approach was conducted for Model B using a different range of hypothetical true effect sizes (i.e., b = 0.15 -0.25, Δ = 0.01). Significance was assessed via a Wald z-test rather than simr's default Kenward-Roger approximation, as the latter's model-comparison procedure is incompatible with the intercept-suppressed model specification. A model with no fixed effects beyond the term of interest has no valid nested reduced-model comparison for Kenward-Roger to construct. The Wald approach is consistent with the inferential framework used elsewhere in the primary analyses.

Table 5 and visualized in Figure 1. Happiness showed robust, large-magnitude synchrony, strongly supporting H1c. Disgust showed a small, positive synchrony estimate that did not reach statistical significance under model-based inference. Although the bootstrapped 95% CI technically excluded zero, [0.002, 0.134], the lower bound sat close enough to the boundary, combined with the non-statistically significant Wald test, that H1b was considered not supported (see Deviations). The sensitivity power analyses (Table 1) provide further context for this determination. This design's MDES for disgust at 80% power was b = 0.10, meaning the observed effect fell below the threshold at which this design could detect an effect with at least 80% power.

table.title: Same-Emotion Synchrony During Laboratory-Based Intimate Partner Aggression
table.research_questions:
1. Do romantic partners show within-dyad, trial-to-trial synchrony (i.e., coupling net of stable between-dyad average level) in anger, disgust, and happiness during a face-to-face, laboratory-based measure of intimate partner aggression?

2. Does the magnitude of anger, disgust, and/or happiness synchrony differ between an immediate-response condition and a forced-break condition? 1a. Within-dyad synchrony for anger will be significantly greater than zero, pooling across conditions.
1b. Within-dyad synchrony for disgust will be significantly greater than zero, pooling across conditions.
1c. Within-dyad synchrony for happiness will be significantly greater than zero, pooling across conditions.
2a. Anger synchrony will be significantly weaker in the forced-break condition than the immediate-response condition.
2b. Disgust synchrony will be significantly weaker in the forced-break condition than the immediate-response condition.
2c. Happiness synchrony will not differ between conditions (i.e., the force break is predicted to selectively disrupt negatively-valenced emotion coupling while leaving positively-valenced emotion coupling intact).
table.datasets_used: I am using the dataset originally reported by McCurry et al. (2024). I will use the data for the Facial Action Coding System analyses regarding the affective facial displays from both participants.
table.data_collection_procedures:
Data collection procedures are well-documented in the original publication for this data: https://www.nature.com/articles/s44271-024-00122-4

McCurry, A. G., May, R. C., & Donaldson, D. I. (2024). Both partners' negative emotion drives aggression during couple's conflict. Communications Psychology, 2, 73. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44271-024-00122-4.
table.manipulated_variables: Participants, at the dyad-level, were randomly assigned to either an immediate-response or forced-break condition. This will be dummy-coded as two mutually exclusive indicators for the two-intercept model structure.
table.measured_variables: Outcome: Trial-level intensity scores for anger, disgust, and happiness (OpenFace/FACS-derived, blast-initiation +/- 1 s window), standardized within-person (M= 0, SD = 1).
table.missing_data_handling:
For reasons unspecified in the original article, but confirmed by independent analysis of the data structure, two of the 53 dyads in the study are incomplete (i.e., have data for only one dyad member). These dyads will be excluded as synchrony analyses require both partners' trial-level scores for every round. These participants will be excluded listwise, yielding a final analysis sample of 51 dyads (11 control, 40 forced-break).

Four of the 51 retained dyads have fewer than 30 rounds, for reasons unspecified in the original article, for at least one partner. In each case, the shorter partner's round set was a clean subset of their partners, so these dyads are retained but trimmed to each dyad's own shared round set. Post-trim, all 51 dyads have identical, matched round sets between partners (verified directly). Final per-dyad trial-round distribution: 47 dyads at full 30 rounds, one dyad at 18 rounds, two dyads at 28 rounds, and one dyad at 29 rounds.
table.prior_knowledge:
I have read the full published manuscript (i.e., McCurry et al., 2024), which includes:
1. The collapsed positive/negative affect composite scores (not the per-emotion breakdown): negative affect predicted higher blast-level selections; forced breaks reduced both negativity and blast level; mediation analyses indicated the forced-break effect on aggression operated through negativity
2. A reported null concurrent partner-correlation result for the collapsed negativity composite, based on a pooled single-level correlation that did not separate within-dyad from between-dyad variance.
3. No escalation at the round level.

All prior work with this dataset may be found on the PreReg_DataCleaning.R file
table.statistical_tests:
Step 1: Descriptive check
-Base rates and between-dyad ICCs for all coded emotions will be examined prior to modeling. This will confirm that (a) anger, disgust, and happiness clear a reasonable floor and show non-trivial between-dyad variance, and (b) sadness, fear, and surprise are viable for exploratory analyses.

Emotions will be considered viable for modeling if it clears a non-floor threshold (i.e., intensity > 0 on at least 5% of trials) and its between-dyad ICC (variance in a random-intercept model) is high enough that a dyad-level random effect has something to capture, rather than the emotion's variance being almost entirely within-person noise. No fixed numeric ICC is prespecified; ICCs will be reported and interpreted in context (i.e., relative to each other across the six emotions) rather than tested against an arbitrary threshold, since no established convention exists for this specific application.

Step 2: Indistinguishability
Before fitting models in Step 3, the assumption that dyad members are indistinguishable will be tested empirically. A model constraining member-level means and variances equal across the two arbitrarily labeled partners will be compared, via a likelihood-ratio test, against an unconstrained model allowing member-specific means and variances to differ freely. A non-statistically significant (i.e., p > .05) LRT will support treating the dyad as indistinguishable, as planned. A statistically significant LRT would indicate the arbitrary P1/P2 labeling is not actually arbitrary and would require revisiting the modeling approach before proceeding to Step 3. This check will be run once per emotion (anger, disgust, happiness), since indistinguishability could hold for one emotion but not another.

Step 3: Random-effects structure check (Model B in Step 4)
Before finalizing Model B (Step 4), whether its random-slope variance should be shared across conditions or allowed to differ by condition (largely due to unequal group sizes) will be tested empirically. Two versions of the interaction model's random-effects terms will be compared via a likelihood-ratio test

#R Code
model_re_shared<-lmer(zEmo_2 ~ -1 + zEmo_1 * condition.b - condition.b + (0 + zEmo_1 | pair_id), data = data, REML = TRUE)

model_re_hetero<-lmer(zEmo_2 ~ -1 + zEmo_1 * condition.b - condition.b + 
          (0 + zEmo_1:condition.b + zEmo_1:condition.b2 || pair_id), data = data, REML = TRUE

anova(model_re_shared, model_re_hetero)

*Note that model_re_hetero's random-effects term uses both condition.b and condition.b2 (two mutually exclusive dummy-coded variables), even though Model B's fixed effects use only condition.b. Obtaining two seperate per-condition variance components (rather than a single shared one) requires two group-specific random-slope terms in the || structure.*

REML is used for this comparison specifically to compare random-effects structures when the fixed effects are identical across the two models being compared. Because this is a boundary test, the standard chi-square LRT p-value is conservative; this will be noted in reporting, and results will be interpreted with that caveat rather than treated as exact. A non-statistically significant LRT support the simpler shared-variance structure; a statistically-significant LRT supports allowing the variance to differ by condition, and the heterogenous structure will be used. This check will be done for each emotion.

Step 4: Primary Models
Two linear mixed models will be fit per emotion (anger, disgust, happiness), each on the trial-matched, within-person-standardized dataset with zEmo_1/zEmo_2 denoting the arbitrarily labeled dyad members' scores for that emotion.

Justification for suppressed intercepts in Models A and B:
Because the emotions are standardized within-person (M = 0, SD = 1) prior to modeling, each individual's own mean is 0 by construction, and each dyad's mean (across the two members) is 0 by construction. Therefore, there is no fixed-effect intercept or random-effect intercept to estimate as both are known to be 0 rather than unknown quantities requiring a parameter. Including them would not bias the synchrony estimate, but would waste degrees of freedom estimating parameters whose value is already fixed by the standardization step, and departs from the definition of the quantity of interest. "-1" suppresses the fixed intercept in the outcome equation. ") +" suppresses the corresponding random intercept in the random-effects term, leaving only the random slope(s) to be estimated. This also carries a second, more specific consequence noted earlier: standardization makes the slope symmetric with respect to which member is coded as P1/P2 (i.e., for standardized variables, B_yx = B_xy = r), which is what allows this specification to respect indistinguishability without requiring a double-entry/pairwise-stacked dataset structure.

Model A - Pooled Synchrony (H1a-c): a single common synchrony slope across conditions:

#R Example Code where Emo is a placeholder for the specific emotion

model_pooled <- lmer(zEmo_2 ~ -1 + zEmo_1 + (0 + zEmo_1 | pair_id), data = data, REML = FLASE)

Model B - condition as moderator (omnibus test of H2a-c): standard moderation specification

#R Code
model_interaction<-lmer(zEmo_2 ~ -1 + zEmo_1*condition.b - condition.b + 
            (0 + zEmo_1 | pair_id) # or heterogenous structure, per Step
            data = data, REML = FALSE
***where condition.b is a single treatment-coded (0 = control, 1 = forced break) dummy; -1 + zEmo_1 * condition.b - condition.b expands to zEmo_1 + zEmo_1:condition.b (main effect of partner's emotion in the control group, plus the interaction term testing whether that slope differs in the forced-break group), with the overall and condition.b main-effect intercepts both correctly suppressed given the within-person-standardization rationale above. Random-effects structure (shown here as shared/simple, matching the original example specification) follows the determination made in Step 3.

Model C - condition-specific synchrony (H2a-c): two-intercept structure, allowing synchrony to differ by condition

#R Code

model_condition <- lmer(zEmo_2 ~ -1 + zEmo_1:condition.b + zEmo_1:condition.bx + (0 + zEmo_1:condition.b + zEmo_1:condition.b2 || pair_id), data = data, REML = FALSE)

**where condition.b/condition.b2 are mutually exclusive dummy codes for immediate response vs. forced break.

*I will not use detrending for round order. Round number in the task is not included as a covariate in either model and the concurrent (same-round) covariance structure is treated as the estimate of interest without adjusting for any linear or other trend across the 30 rounds. This decision is deliberate: round number does not map onto elapsed time in a comparable way across conditions. Round 15, for example, represents a different amount of elapsed session time depending on condition and dyad. Detrending on round number would therefore not cleanly separate a "time in session" effect from condition itself, and could introduce a confound rather than remove one. Round-order effects are consequently not modeled or tested.*

H2a-c testing structure: Model B's zEmo_1:condition.b interaction term is the primary, omnibus test of H2a-c. A statistically significant interaction (i.e., two-tailed p < .05) indicates condition moderates synchrony for that emotion. Model C is reported alongside it as the simple-slopes decomposition, giving each condition's synchrony estimate directly rather than requiring reconstruction. As a convergence check, a likelihood-ratio test comparing Model B (or Model C) against Model A will be reported. This should agree with the interaction term's statistical significance and serves as the robustness check on the omnibus conclusions rather than an independent test. All three model are fit with REML = FALSE to keep likelihoods comparable for the LRT.
table.inference_criteria:
H1a-c
For each emotion, the pooled synchrony fixed effect (i.e., zEmo_1 slope in Model A) will be interpreted as a correlation coefficient and support the hypothesis if it is statistically significantly greater than 0 (i.e., p < .05; two-tailed), using model-based standard errors as the default and bootstrapped confidence intervals as the robustness check.

H2a-b
The condition difference in synchrony will be interpreted as supported if Model B's zEmo_1:condition.b interaction term is statistically significant (i.e., two-tailed p < .05). Model C's two condition-specific slopes will be reported alongside it to characterize the direction and within-condition magnitude of the effect, and the LRT comparing Model B against Model A will be reported as a convergence check. 

H2c
H2c predicts the absence of a meaningful difference and is tested as formal statistical equivalence rather than inferred from a non-statistically significant difference (Lakens, 2017). Using the two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure applied to Model B's zEmo_1:condition.b interaction coefficient for happiness

boot_ci_90<-confint(model_interaction, method = "boot", nsim = 2000, level = .90, parm = "zEmo_1:condition.b")

The equivalence bound is set at delta = .10 on the standardized slope/correlation scale, used as a default in the absence of any prior study to anchor this specific parameter. H2c will be supported if the resulting 90% confidence interval falls entirely within [-0.10,0.10]. If the CI is wider, but also does not exclude zero, result will will be reported as inconclusive.

***Multiple Comparisons***
Three emotions are tested for each H1 and H2, for a total of six confirmatory test. No correction for multiple comparisons will be applied, since each emotion represents a distinct, independently motivated a priori hypothesis rather than an exploratory sweep across interchangeable outcomes. Results will be reported for all three emotions regardless of statistical significance.
table.reliability_and_robustness_testing: Given the original authors' own finding of significant non-normality across their measures, robustness of inferential conclusions to non-normality will be checked via bootstrapped confidence intervals on the key synchrony estimates and slope-difference contrasts (e.g., lme4::bootMer() or confint(..., method = "boot")), rather than relying solely on default Wald/ML-based inference. Where bootstrapped and model-based inference disagree on significance at α = .05, the bootstrapped result will be treated as authoritative and this will be noted explicitly in reporting.
table.exploratory_analyses: If base rates/ICCs support modeling (Step 1), sadness, fear, and surprise synchrony will be reported as exploratory analyses given the weaker theoretical case relative to anger, disgust, and happiness.

3 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

info.title: Same-Emotion Synchrony During Laboratory-Based Intimate Partner Aggression

author.affiliation:
Department of Psychology
								
									Richmond
									VA
									USA

text.text: The moment-to-moment coupling of partners' facial expressions (i.e., synchrony) is a core channel of nonverbal coordination, yet it has rarely been measured during overt conflict.

Using recorded facial expressions during a laboratory-based intimate partner aggression task, I estimated trial-level, same-emotion expressive synchrony, decomposed from between-dyad similarity, for 51 dyads (N = 102 participants).
Confirmatory analyses focused on emotional synchrony for anger, disgust, and happiness and tested whether a forced-break manipulation moderated synchrony.
Happiness synchrony was robust.
Anger synchrony was not detected.
Disgust synchrony was not reliably distinguished from zero, though statistical power was limited.
Contrary to the preregistered hypotheses, condition moderated only happiness synchrony, and in the opposite direction to what was anticipated.
Positive coupling was stronger in the forced-break condition than the immediate-response condition, rather than remaining stable.
Structured pauses during conflict may afford partners an opportunity to coordinate positive affect rather than serving only to interrupt negative affect.
Altogether, partners' positive emotional expressions during a laboratory-based intimate partner aggression task couple, and this coupling is sensitive to the structure of the interaction.
Intimate partner aggression (IPA)-an attempt to harm a current or former romantic partner who is motivated to avoid that harm-is often motivated by affect.

During conflict, each partner's affect is continuously shaped by the other's, and models of IPA increasingly locate IPA's drivers in the dyad rather than the individual (Bartholomew & Cobb, 2011; Capaldi et al., 2012).
text.formatted: During conflict, each partner's affect is continuously shaped by the other's, and models of IPA increasingly locate IPA's drivers in the dyad rather than the individual <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bartholomew & Cobb, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Capaldi et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: How tightly two partners track one another's emotions (i.e., their emotional synchrony) may bear on whether conflicts escalate or subside.
Synchrony has seldom been measured directly in this setting, and whether interventions that reduce aggression do so partly by altering synchrony remains unknown.

In what follows, I detail my examination of same-emotion synchrony during a laboratory-based IPA task and test whether a forced-break manipulation during the IPA task moderates same-emotion synchrony. McCurry et al. (2024) provided direct support for a dyadic account of IPA by using a face-to-face modification of a competitive reaction-time task (Taylor, 1967; Warburton & Bushman, 2019), in which romantic partners delivered aversive noise blasts to one another across repeated rounds.

text.text: Both partners' negative affect, coded from facial expression, predicted the intensity of aggressive behavior.
Furthermore, a forced-break manipulation that inserted a mandatory pause between provocation and response reduced aggression with the reduction mediated by lowered negative affect.

The manipulation was motivated by a Violence Escalation Cycle (Anderson et al., 2008; Dewall & Anderson, 2011) account, which posits that unchecked reciprocal negativity builds across an interaction until it culminates in aggressive behavior.
text.formatted: The manipulation was motivated by a Violence Escalation Cycle <ref type="bibr">(Anderson et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Dewall & Anderson, 2011)</ref> account, which posits that unchecked reciprocal negativity builds across an interaction until it culminates in aggressive behavior.

text.text: A forced pause is presumed to interrupt the cycle before it peaks.
Mean-level negative affect, though, is only one way partners' emotions can be interdependent (e.g., Sels et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Mean-level negative affect, though, is only one way partners' emotions can be interdependent (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Sels et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A conceptually distinct quantity is synchrony: the trial-to-trial coupling of one partner's emotional expression with the other's, estimated net of each dyad's stable average level of that emotion.
Synchrony indexes the moment-to-moment coordination, or covariation, of affect rather than its overall quantity.
Importantly, the two can diverge.
A couple may express little negativity on average yet track each other closely when it does arise.
Whether such coupling matters, and how, is not neutral a question.

Research on close relationships often treats partners' emotions as a coupled dynamic system whose coordination can regulate or dysregulate the couple's interactions by dampening arousal toward a shared equilibrium or amplifying it (Butler & Randall, 2013).
text.formatted: Research on close relationships often treats partners' emotions as a coupled dynamic system whose coordination can regulate or dysregulate the couple's interactions by dampening arousal toward a shared equilibrium or amplifying it <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Butler & Randall, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: A well-documented case of amplification is negative affect reciprocity, the tendency for one partner's negativity to elicit the other's negativity.
Chains of reciprocated negativity escalate conflict and reliably forecast dissatisfaction and dissolution (Gottman & Levenson, 1992; Levenson & Gottman, 1983).
text.formatted: Chains of reciprocated negativity escalate conflict and reliably forecast dissatisfaction and dissolution <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Gottman & Levenson, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Levenson & Gottman, 1983)</ref>.

text.text: Coordination of positive affect carries the opposite implication, reflecting the mutual attunement through which partners can co-regulate (Butler & Randall, 2013).
text.formatted: Coordination of positive affect carries the opposite implication, reflecting the mutual attunement through which partners can co-regulate <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Butler & Randall, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Emotional synchrony is therefore valenced in its likely consequences.
While coupled negative states may mark a pathway to escalation, coupled positive states may mark a pathway to repair.
Of the emotions coded by McCurry et al. (2024), three emotions representing both negatively-and positively-valenced states pose the clearest rationale for examination.
text.formatted: Of the emotions coded by <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">McCurry et al. (2024)</ref>, three emotions representing both negatively-and positively-valenced states pose the clearest rationale for examination.

text.text: Anger and disgust are negatively-valenced emotions which are central to popular theoretical approaches to examining aggressive behavior (Anderson & Bushman, 2002; Bondü & Richter, 2016; Haidt, 2003), and approaching them separately respects a well-documented distinction in their elicitors and response tendencies (Rozin et al., 1999).

text.text: Anger synchrony would index shared approach-oriented hostility (Carver & Harmon-Jones, 2009), whereas disgust synchrony would index a shared response of rejection or withdrawal (Rozin & Fallon, 1987).

text.text: Happiness represents a positively-valenced emotion whose role in aggressive behavior is less clear.
While positive affect is often assumed to dampen aggressive responding, it is not uniformly protective.
Aggression can itself be rewarding, and positive feeling is increasingly implicated as a correlate and cause of aggressive behaviors (Chester, 2017; Chester, in press).
text.formatted: Aggression can itself be rewarding, and positive feeling is increasingly implicated as a correlate and cause of aggressive behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Chester, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Chester, in press)</ref>.

text.text: Happiness synchrony is an ambiguous case; shared positive expressions during conflict may reflect co-regulatory attunement, or a mutual and rewarding investment in the exchange itself.

To my knowledge, no prior work has estimated trial-level same-emotion synchrony, separated from between-dyad similarity and modeled per emotion, during laboratory-based IPA, nor tested whether a forced-break manipulation moderates synchrony.

The present study addresses both questions through a secondary analysis of the main study reported by McCurry et al. (2024), testing whether anger, disgust, and happiness show within-dyad coupling above stable average levels, and whether that coupling differs between the immediate-response and forced-break conditions.

text.text: I advanced two sets of preregistered hypotheses regarding these research questions.
For the existence of same-emotion synchrony, I predicted detectable sameemotion synchrony larger than zero in anger (H1a), disgust (H1b), and happiness (H1c).
(2024) that forced breaks operate by interrupting negatively-valenced emotion coupling while leaving positively-valenced emotion coupling intact.
I predicted that forced breaks would weaken anger synchrony (H2a) and disgust synchrony (H2b) relative to immediate responses, while happiness synchrony would remain unaffected by condition (H2c).
Because H2c represents an equivalence claim, it was evaluated against a preregistered equivalence-testing procedure rather than by failure to reject a null hypothesis.

text.text: Study recruitment occurred through the University of St.
Andrews' (St.
Andrews, Scotland) participant recruitment and memo systems.
Interested individuals completed an online pre-screening survey to assess inclusion criteria (i.e., over the age of majority in Scotland, currently in a romantic relationship).
If deemed eligible, potential participants were scheduled with their romantic partner to attend a laboratory-based experimental session.
At the beginning of the laboratory-based session, participants provided their consent, though were left blind to the fact that the study measured intimate partner aggression.
After providing their consent, dyad members were randomly assigned, as a unit, to either an immediate-response or forced-break condition, which applies to the aggression measure detailed next.
Participants were shown a brief demonstration of a face-to-face (FTF) version of the Competitive Reaction Time Task (CRTT; Warburton & Bushman, 2019).
text.formatted: Participants were shown a brief demonstration of a face-to-face (FTF) version of the Competitive Reaction Time Task (CRTT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Warburton & Bushman, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: After the demonstration, participants completed 30 rounds of the FTF-CRTT.
During the game, both romantic partners were in the same room, standing at separate monitors, but facing each other with an unobstructed view of their partner's face.
During the task, participants competed to press a button faster than their opponent.
In rounds where the discrepancy between the button press was 100 ms or lower, the winner was chosen at random.
In the immediate-response condition, the winner immediately selected the volume of the noise blast to be delivered to their partner, ranging from 75 db to 110 db.
In the forced-break condition, the winner waited either 5 s, 10 s, or 15 s before making their decision (break lengths were collapsed for analysis; see Data Analysis Plan).
Video recording was continuous throughout the FTF-CRTT.

text.text: Trial-level emotion intensity scores were standardized within-participants (i.e., M = 0, SD = 1) prior to modeling.

This standardization enables the resulting synchrony estimate to be symmetric with respect to arbitrary partner labeling, which was central to the modeling approach adopted for indistinguishable dyads.
Four of the dyads in the final sample had fewer than 30 rounds of the FTF-CRTT, for reasons unspecified in the original article.
In each case, the shorter partner's round set was a subset of their partner's, and these dyads were retained by trimming to each dyad's own shared round set rather than excluded.
This was considered to be a deviation from the preregistration.
Dyad members were treated as indistinguishable.

Partner labeling was assigned at random within each dyad, independent of any substantive variable, since no systematic, theoretically meaningful distinction between partners was available in the sample.

Same-emotion synchrony was operationalized as the within-dyad, trial-to-trial (i.e., concurrent) covariation between partners' standardized emotion intensity scores estimated via linear mixed models with dyad as a random effect.
This approach decomposes concurrent covariation into a within-dyad component and a between-dyad component, addressing a limitation of simple pooled correlations, which conflate the two.

Prior to modeling, base rates (i.e., percentage of trials with intensity > 0) and between-dyad intraclass correlations (ICCs, from a random-intercept model on raw, unstandardized intensity) were examined for all coded emotions.
text.formatted: Prior to modeling, base rates (i.e., percentage of trials with intensity > 0) and between-dyad intraclass correlations (ICCs, from a random-intercept model on raw, unstandardized intensity) were examined for all coded emotions.

text.text: An emotion was considered viable for modeling if it cleared a non-floor base rate (i.e., intensity > 0 on at least 5% of trials) and showed non-trivial between-dyad variance relative to the other emotions.
text.formatted: An emotion was considered viable for modeling if it cleared a non-floor base rate (i.e., intensity > 0 on at least 5% of trials) and showed non-trivial between-dyad variance relative to the other emotions.

text.text: I did not specify a fixed, numeric ICC threshold as there is not a widelyestablished convention for this application.

For each emotion retained after assessing base rates and ICCs, a model constraining partner-level means and variance equal across the two arbitrarily labeled dyad members was compared to an unconstrained model allowing member-specific means and variances to differ freely.
This check was conducted on raw intensity scores, since within-person standardization would trivially equate means and variances by construction.

For the condition-moderation model (Model B, below), whether the random slope variance should be estimated as shared across conditions or allowed to differ by condition was tested empirically via likelihood-ratio test, comparing a shared-variance specification against a heterogenous-variance specification, for each retained emotion.
Three linear mixed models were fit per emotion.
Model A estimated a single pooled synchrony slope across conditions, testing whether same-emotion synchrony differed from zero.

Model B tested condition as a moderator of synchrony via a dummycoded condition variable (control = 0, experimental =1), with the coefficient for the interaction serving as the omnibus test of whether synchrony differed between the immediate-response and forced-break conditions.
As in McCurry et al. (2024), all forced-break conditions were collapsed into a single forced-break condition.
text.formatted: As in <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">McCurry et al. (2024)</ref>, all forced-break conditions were collapsed into a single forced-break condition.

text.text: Model C decomposed Model B's interaction into condition-specific simple slopes, reported alongside Model B to characterize the direction and magnitude of any condition effect.
This model included two dummy-coded condition variables, one was the same variable used in Model B while the other reversed the scoring.
This approach provides separate estimates of covariation in each condition.
Fixed intercepts were omitted from all models, as within-participant standardization fixes each individual's and each dyad's mean at exactly zero, leaving no intercept to estimate.
As preregistered, the data were not detrended for the effect of time.

Round number in the task is not included as a covariate in any model and the concurrent covariance structure is treated as the estimate of interest without adjusting for any linear or non-linear trend across the 30 rounds.
This decision was made due to the fact that the round number does not map onto elapsed time in a comparable way across conditions.
Detrending on round numbers would not cleanly separate a time effect from condition itself, and could introduce a confound rather than remove one.
Fixed-effect statistical significance tests used Satterthwaite-approximated degrees of freedom.

Given evidence of non-normality in facial-affect intensity scores reported by McCurry et al. (2024), bootstrapped confidence intervals were computed as a robustness check on all primary fixed-effect estimates.

text.text: Where bootstrapped and model-based inferences disagreed, the bootstrapped result was treated as authoritative, per the preregistered decision rule.

For the directional hypothesis predicting equivalence in condition effects for happiness synchrony (i.e., H2c), a two one-sided tests (TOST) equivalence procedure was used (Lakens, 2017), with an equivalence bound of Δ = 0.10 on the standardized slope scale.

text.text: Three deviations from the preregistered analysis plan were deemed necessary during data preparation and analysis.
Full details may be found in the Supplementary Materials.
First, a subset of participants showed zero within-participant variance on a given emotion, most substantially for fear and anger.
This was not anticipated in the preregistered exclusion criteria.

Dyads containing such a participant were excluded from that emotion's models specifically, yielding a reduced analytic sample for anger (n = 39 dyads) relative to disgust and happiness (n = 51 dyads).

Second, the preregistered indistinguishability check returned a statistically significant likelihood-ratio test for three emotions, which by the preregistered decision rule would have required revisiting the modeling approach.
Diagnostic follow-up traced this to raw-scale variance heterogeneity unrelated to the standardized-scale synchrony estimates the models actually report.

This conclusion was confirmed by 25 independent re-randomizations of partner labeling rather than relied upon as reasoning alone, after which the originally preregistered modelling approach was retained.
Third, for disgust specifically, the bootstrapped confidence interval technically excluded zero (i.e., lower limit = 0.002) while the corresponding Wald test did not reach statistical significance.

Given the boundaryadjacent lower bound of the interval, this was interpreted as a non-supported effect, departing from the preregistered rule prioritizing bootstrapped inference when the two methods disagree.

The Wald approach is consistent with the inferential framework used elsewhere in the primary analyses.

Anger and disgust showed no evidence of condition moderation in either direction.
Together, these findings suggest a different account of how forced breaks during conflict may operate than the account motivating the preregistered hypotheses.

I originally predicted that forced breaks would function by selectively interrupting negatively-valenced emotion (i.e., anger, disgust) coupling while leaving positivelyvalenced emotion (i.e., happiness) coupling intact.

This account was grounded in the Violence Escalation Cycle (Anderson et al., 2008; Dewall & Anderson, 2011) and the broader theoretical framing of McCurry et al. (2024), whose mediation analyses indicated forced breaks reduce aggressive behavior via reduced negative affect.

The results do not support the specific coupling-disruption mechanism I originally proposed.
Anger and disgust showed no detectable coupling to disrupt in the first place, and happiness coupling was amplified.
One plausible alternative account is that forced breaks function less as an interruption of negative escalation and more as a shared coordination opportunity.

A brief pause may allow partners to re-align on positive affect together, whether through eye contact, a shared laugh or smile, or simply time removed from the competitive framing of the task (e.g., Arias-Sarah et al., 2024; Delgado et al., 2023; Kurtz & Algoe, 2015).

text.text: The reframing shifts the proposed function of the break from disrupting an existing negative coupling to creating an occasion for positive coupling.
Future research should test this proposed mechanism by varying what partners do during the pause, not only whether a pause occurs.
The absence of anger and disgust synchrony might be attributable to a lack of statistical power and may not serve as positive evidence against the coupling.
Both emotions occurred at low base rates during the task, limiting the opportunity to detect coupling even where it existed.
Anger was additionally floored for a substantial share of the sample; 12 dyads contained at least one participant with no variance in anger across trials and could not be modeled.
With so little non-floor signal, the anger models were poorly positioned to recover coupling of any plausible magnitude, and the resulting null result is uninformative about the underlying effect.
Disgust was constrained by a similarly narrow, low-intensity distribution.
Several limitations warrant discussion.
Most fundamentally, the present study does not examine the aggressive behaviors during the task.
Whether same-emotion coupling relates to the intensity, likelihood, or form of aggression is a question the present design cannot address.
The evidence reported here should not be interpreted as evidence that synchrony promotes or mitigates IPA perpetration.
Estimating whether synchrony relates to aggressive behavior within this dataset is not straightforward.
Synchrony is a dyad-level quantity whereas each trial yields a single directed aggression outcome.
A dyad-level association would rest on a maximum of 51 dyads using per-dyad coupling estimates that are imprecise.
This remains an open question deserving of rigorous investigation.
Additionally, the condition cells were small and highly asymmetric.
As the present work is a secondary analysis, the original design of the study was calibrated for meanlevel aggression and its affective drivers, not synchrony.
The present work inherits a design optimized for those aims rather than for detecting differences in synchrony.
Future work should use the effect sizes reported here to conduct a priori power analyses for primary data collection calibrated to questions related to synchrony.
Because anger and disgust were floored by relatively low base rates, future studies should consider designs that elicit these emotions at rates permitting reliable estimation.
Furthermore, the synchrony estimated here is facial-expressive and should not be conflated with physiological or autonomic synchrony.
Future multi-method approaches may combine the facial-expressive synchrony estimates with cardiac or electrodermal synchrony.
This study offers a preliminary estimate of same-emotion expressive synchrony during a laboratory-based IPA task, decomposed from between-dyad similarity and modeled separately by emotion.
Happiness synchrony was robust.
Anger and disgust synchrony were not detected.
Importantly, the design was better positioned to establish the happiness estimate than to rule out the anger and disgust estimates.
The forcedbreak manipulation did not dampen negative-emotion coupling as predicted.
Instead, the manipulation amplified happiness coupling, inviting a reconsideration of what such pauses afford partners rather than what they interrupt.

text.text: This was treated as a deviation from the preregistration.
The preregistered exclusion criteria did not anticipate participants who showed zero within-participant variance on a given emotion across trials.
Such cases occurred, most substantially for fear and anger.

Because trial-level emotion intensity scores were standardized within-person prior to modeling, a series with no within-person variance cannot be standardized as the operation requires division by the within-person standard deviation.
Additionally, this carries no information about trial-to-trial coupling.
I excluded any dyad containing such a participant from that specific emotion's models only, rather than removing the dyad from all analyses.
The rationale is that the problem is emotionspecific.
A participant who is flat on anger may vary normally on happiness.
A listwise exclusion across all emotions would discard usable data for no methodological gain.
The consequence is that analytic samples differ by emotion.
The anger models rest on 39 dyads, whereas the disgust and happiness models rest on the full final same.
This exclusion, and the resulting emotion-specific sample sizes, propagate into the emotionspecific power analyses reported in the main text.

For screening which emotions were viable for modeling, I preregistered attention to base rates and between-dyad variance but did not preregister a fixed numeric threshold on the intraclass correlation (ICC).

I applied a base-rate floor (intensity greater than zero on at least 5% of trials) as a hard criterion, but evaluated between-dyad variance relative to the other coded emotions rather than against a preregistered ICC cutoff.
I made this choice because no widely established ICC convention exists for this application, to my knowledge, and any fixed cutoff would have been largely arbitrary.
This is best characterized as a clarification of an underspecified element of the preregistered analysis plan rather than a contradiction.

I preregistered a check comparing a constrained model (equating partner-level means and variances across the two arbitrarily labeled dyad members against an unconstrained model, with the decision rule that a statistically significant likelihood-ratio test would require revisiting the modeling approach.
The test was statistically significant for three emotions (anger, disgust, and the exploratory surprise).
Following the preregistered rule literally would have prompted a change in approach.

Diagnostic follow-up instead traced the statistically significant result to heterogeneity in the rawscale variances between the arbitrarily labeled dyad members, a feature that does not affect the standardized-scale synchrony estimate the models actually report.
The indistinguishability check is necessarily conducted on raw intensity scores because within-person standardization would trivially equate means and variances by construction.
The reported coupling estimates are computed on the standardized scale.
To confirm that the reported estimates were not sensitive to this raw-scale heterogeneity, I re-estimated the models across 25 independent re-randomization of partner labeling.
The synchrony estimates were stable across all 25 relabelings.
On this basis, I retained the originally registered modelling approach for all affected emotions.
This is a departure from the preregistered decision rule.
I believe it to be justified because the triggering condition was diagnosed as irrelevant to the quantities being estimated.
For the pooled disgust synchrony estimate, the two inference methods disagreed.
The bootstrapped 95% confidence interval technically excluded zero (lower limit of 0.002) while the corresponding Wald test did not reach statistical significance (p = .054).
Under the preregistered decision rule prioritizing bootstrapped inference, this pattern would have supported H1b.
I instead interpreted the effect as not supported, deviating from that rule.

The reasoning combined three considerations: the lower bound of the bootstrapped interval sat immediately adjacent to zero, the Wald test was not statistically significant, and the sensitivity power analysis indicated the observed effect fell below the minimum detectable effect size this design could detect with approximately 80% power.
Read together, these point to an underpowered, inconclusive result.
The decision affects the verdict on H1b, which is reported as not supported, and it is framed throughout as an inconclusive result.
